text: The House will come to order. Members, please take your seats. Head page. The House is now in session. All persons not entitled to privileges of the floor, please retire to the gallery.

The members will rise and be led in prayer by Dr. George Anderson, Senior Pastor, Presbyterian Church, Roanoke, and remain standing for the Pledge of Allegiance of the Flag of the United States of America, which will be led by the Delegate from Alexandria, Delegate Herring. Let us pray.

Holy One of justice and mercy, we bow before you mindful of the weight and privilege of leadership. You have entrusted this body with shaping laws for a diverse and spirited commonwealth. Grant these delegates grace to listen carefully, to speak truthfully, and to act with integrity.

May their work continue to set an example worthy of this chamber, showing that conviction and civility can dwell together and that disagreement need not become disdain. In negotiation, grant them creativity, and in compromise, grant them wisdom, for we know that even imperfect agreements can advance the common good.
Bless this commonwealth, our nation, and the world, that the inheritance of coming generations may be greater justice, peace, and kindness in the way we live together. Amen.
The members will answer the roll call by indicating their presence on the electronic voting board.
Clerk will close the roll. Mr. Speaker, a quorum is present. Pursuant to House Rule 3, I've examined and approved the General House of Delegates for February 19, 2026.

Most of the resolutions under Rule 39 pursuant to the provisions of Rule 40 are now in order. Does the clerk have any additional announcements or communications? No, sir, not at this time. Accordingly in this first portion of the morning hour, pursuant to House Rule 40, speaker, request to use your request to speak button for the agenda items listed for reference up on the voting board.
Delegate from Richmond, Delegate Carr. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise for an introduction and then a motion. The delegate has the floor. Thank you, sir. Thank you, members and colleagues.

Joining us today in the gallery are members from the Junior League of Richmond, and I ask them to please stand now. The Junior League celebrates its centennial, marking 100 years of service to the greater Richmond community. Founded in 1926 by 59 young women, the JLR has advanced women's leadership and driven social impact through volunteerism, professional development, and community action.

I'm proud to say I'm a sustaining member of the Richmond Junior League and know that But some of my colleagues have enjoyed shopping at their consignment store, the clothes rack here in Kerrytown. There's a strong tradition of maternal and child advocacy in the Junior League of Richmond, including lobbyists, lobbying for the Mother's Aid Bill, which helped establish Well Baby and Immunology clinics across the city, and cemented Virginia as a participant in one of the nation's first major federal welfare programs.

During World War II, the Junior League raised $150,000 over $2 million today for war bonds and supported service members through weekly programs. In the Richmond we know today, the League has played a foundational role by supporting the creation of the Science Museum of Virginia, Children's Theatre of Richmond, Greater Richmond Child Advocacy Center, and the Senior Center of Richmond.

The League continues to value women helping women through partnerships with local nonprofits focused on addressing domestic violence, job opportunity, foster care, under-resourced public schools, affordable housing, and improving access to child care.
Please join me in honoring the Junior League of Richmond for a century of service, leadership, and community impact, and welcome them today. Welcome.

Welcome to the Capitol today. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. And with that said, I would like to move that we take House Joint Resolution 142 up out of order, and I ask that we move its adoption. Clerk will report a resolution. House Joint Resolution 142 commending the Junior League of Richmond.

All those in favor of adopting House Joint Resolution 142 commending the Junior League of Richmond will say aye. Those opposed, no. The motion is agreed to. Congratulations. The delegate from Roanoke, Delegate McNamara. Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of an introduction. The delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, leading us in prayer this morning was Dr. George C. Anderson in the back of our galley. Gallery, senior pastor of Second Presbyterian Church in Roanoke City. There he serves as the seventh senior pastor in the history of Second Presbyterian Church, where he has been preaching since 1998. In recent years, Second Presbyterian raised more than $1.7 million to renovate shelter houses for community members in need, as well as to support the Presbyterian Community Center that serves Roanoke residents.

Pastor Anderson is a graduate of St. Andrews Presbyterian College in Laurenburg, North Carolina, and Union Presbyterian Seminary here in Richmond. Dr. Anderson is involved in every aspect of church life with an emphasis on preaching, teaching, visiting, and staff oversight.
Pastor Anderson and his wife Millie have three wonderful daughters, Paige, Rachel, and Virginia, and two beautiful grandchildren. I ask you all to join me in giving him a very warm house welcome.
Welcome, welcome to the Capitol, and thank you for that wonderful prayer this morning. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Delegate from Chesapeake, Delegate Leftwich. Mr. Speaker, I rise for a motion.

The delegate has the floor. And I'd like to speak to that motion after I make it. Mr. Speaker, I move that when we adjourn today, we move, we adjourn in the memory and honor of Downer Road Delegate Barry D. Knight.

The delegate has the floor. Speaking of the motion. I hope I can get through this. While we will forever know Barry, a delegate, Barry Knight, as Delegate Knight, or the Honorable Barry D. Knight, or as former chair of the Appropriations Committee, first and foremost, he was a friend, and that is how I choose to remember him.

Barry's life was full of passion and hobbies. He loved flying his helicopter, and when we would go up, he would go through all the safety protocols and safety checks, regardless of whether everything was apparently just fine. During the summer, he spent time in Corrova, which is an area of the beach that's all sand roads, all four-wheel drive.

And we were coming up on an intersection one day, and he said, Jay, I want you to look to the right. I'm going to look to the left. And if you see anybody coming, let me know. If not, I'm going to gun it through the intersection. I said, well, why, Barry? Why don't we just pull up the intersection like normal people do and stop and look?

He goes, I don't have any brakes. Apparently, safety protocols for aviation did not apply to vehicles in the Outer Banks. He had a beautiful home in Marathon with his cousin, Cousin Rudy. He hunted and fished all over the U.S., but his favorite was bone fishing in the Bahamas.

And he rode his Harley in all lower 48 states. When someone passes, you always have questions, things you wish you had asked that person during their life. Mine would be, Barry, have you ever been a paid actor in a Dos Equis commercial?

With his weathered face, beard, mustache, and exploits, he certainly was an interesting man. If I stop now, you would think Barry lived a pretty comfortable life financially, perhaps in his later years. But that wasn't until he scratched and clawed his way up the ladder of life.

I'll touch on that a bit more in a few minutes. But I'll simply say what I just described was about living, sharing his blessings with others, and bringing people together. He routinely had large dinners at his house in Pungo.

He had an open door in Corovo, a marathon, always invited people to stop by anytime, announced or unannounced. He was always ready to share a meal, cocktail, cigar, and most certainly laughter. He routinely took young kids on helicopter rides, showing them the northern beaches of the Outer Banks, showing them the remnants of old wrecks and sandbars that paralleled the shore.

More than once, he medevaced an injured person to Virginia Beach, and at more unfortunate times, when someone was missing in the surf, he joined the search by air. Barry was a generous man, sharing his gifts he had been blessed with.

Not long ago, I was in a duck blind with six other people. The seventh was in the home cooking breakfast because he was smart enough to sit in the middle of a body of water at 13 degrees. I looked around and realized that I didn't know any of these guys three or four years ago.

I met them all through Barry. On a recent quail hunt, I was with a different six guys, and the proprietor asked, how do y'all know each other? We all kind of looked up and said in unison pretty much the same thing.

Barry's the common denominator. We all met through him. I was on a fishing trip last year with yet a different group, and I had the same realization. I could go on. The point is, Barry had a gift of bringing people together and making friends, all predicated upon integrity, trust, and loyalty.

His word was his bond. In remembering Barry, who was affectionately referred to as the mayor of Pungo, it is quintessential to understand where he came from. Barry's roots in the Commonwealth run deep, and he traced his lineage to Thomas Savage.

He immigrated at age 13 as a cabin boy to Christopher Newport on the first supply mission to Jamestown in 1608. At some point, Thomas was, and I quote, gifted to Chief Powhatan. And this is how the story goes according to Barry.

A couple Englishmen at Chief Powhatan were sitting around, probably drinking corn mash brewed by Delegate Ballard's predecessors. One Englishman said, you know, it would be really cool if we take an Indian back to England. Powhatan paused, mused, and agreed that the Motaki could travel to England, but he insisted, in exchange, that his tribe hold an Englishman.

The Englishman thought, looked around, and said, sure, take the cabin boy. They thought to themselves, nobody's going to miss him. But Tom, like any good farmer from Pungo, took these lemons, life dealt him, and made lemonade. He learned the native language and culture and became an important resource for communication and Indian-English relations.

Tom lived a fruitful life and is buried at Bruton Parish Episcopal Church Cemetery in Williamsburg. Although I find this genealogy interesting, there's a reason I tell you this. Through unforeseen circumstances and unfamiliar culture and language, Tom Savage brought people with different backgrounds together.

More than 350 years later, and then more than 60 miles from Jamestown, whether you're in Pungo or Richmond, Barry did the same thing through his personal business and public life. Barry attended Kempstow High School in Virginia Beach and earned his undergraduate master's and doctoral degree in the College of Life and Hard Knocks.

If Barry were here now, he'd probably tell you he didn't have the best male role model in the home growing up and acknowledged that he often wondered how the family would make ends meet. Although Barry had a devoted mother and siblings, in part, he began fending for himself at the age of 14 when he began working eye jobs as a farmhand for Mr. Brown.

After high school, he continued with farm work, supplemented his income during the summer as a long-haul truck driver. By his account, the first house he rented wasn't fit for habitation, indicating that within a month or two of him moving out, it collapsed.

And I mean, it literally fell to the ground. Not bulldozed, but fell to the ground. Nevertheless, he was happy, having said, it was a roof over my head when I needed one, and as only a budget guy could appreciate, it was cheap. All Barry knew was how to work, and he worked hard.

At the age of 26, he bought his first farm. No bank would loan him money, but Mr. Brown did, because he knew Barry's work ethic and believed in him. This gives rise to my second question. I'd like to know the first name of the man who helped Barry become the person he became.
Barry always, to the day he passed, referred to this man as Mr. Brown. Surely he had respect, admiration, and love for this man. And what seemed unimportant before has been curious now.

As we mourn here, I'm sure they are talking hops, parlies, and hogs in heaven. Barry went from working several jobs to one, farming, where he worked 12 hours a day, six days a week, and half a day on Sunday for decades, until he gradually eased out of the farming business and sold much of the 640 acres of farmland he had accumulated.

It was through this hog business that Barry honed his skill to haggle and negotiate. After one transaction, he was sitting at the closing table, and the buyer's lawyer looked at him and said, are you happy with the sale? And Barry replied, well, it's not exactly what I was expecting, but yes, I'm happy. What he didn't say out loud was that the purchase price was exactly two times more than what he would have accepted. Barry brought his craftiness and life experiences to the House of Deluxe in 2009, becoming chair of the House Appropriations from 2022 to 2024,

and has received accolades from governors, former chairs of appropriation, and others as having masterful knowledge of and skillfully crafting Virginia's billion-dollar budget, leading one executive of a Fortune 500 company to observe that in the financial sector, companies typically focus on numbers, but that Barry focused on strategy. I could go on about Barry's contributions to Virginia Beach, Chesapeake, Norfolk, Hampton Roads, and the Commonwealth, the roads, bridges, mergers, and buildings that all have its fingerprints, but what I admire and care for
the most about Barry is his friendship and his devotion to family. Barry, in his words, married his one love and beautiful wife, Paul. Together they raised three boys, Hunter, Kyle, and Forrest,

all three of whom have the pleasure of knowing, all of whom are fine men. They do have the same and have started a new generation of knights, and these values mirror Barry and Paul's faith, integrity, loyalty, and work ethic. Meaningful relationships, whether it's with a spouse, a child, a family member, a neighbor, or a colleague, require time and effort. I think,

and I think we all try to build those relationships, but it just comes natural to some people. Personality is infectious, and their bandwidth to interact with others is limitless. Barry was one of these people. Although I call Barry one of my best friends, for me that probably describes a group of maybe a handful of people but barry had dozens if not a hundred or more best friends he just had a gift he was the one person who could tell a clean joke make people laugh as much the 20th time as he told it as he did the first time he told it his jokes were so corny but he became

so excited and tickled with himself you start laughing before he ever got to the bunch line barry and i started out as two guys in the same party representing portions of chesapeake we got They know each other, they had little caucus members, and later served on the same committee.

These things led to many conversations, which led to hanging out and socializing together. Without even realizing that we became friends. We hunted, fished, and carried on like guys do. You know, a little bit of machoism. And one day, one of us used the F word.

You know, the thing guys have a hard time talking about. We talked about our faith. And Barry was a man of faith. He is a believer, and he knew Christ as a Savior. And while his family lost a husband, father, and brother, the Commonwealth lost a phenomenal and effective leader, and countless people lost a friend.

I know he's in a better place, free of pain and the troubles of this world, and has a new set of friends in heaven, all of whom, no doubt, will enjoy his company and laugh at the same corny jokes we laughed at. Mr. Speaker, before I yield the floor to the delegate from Richmond City, Delegate McQuinn, a final thought, I find solace in a passage penned by Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a German pastor, a theologian.

No one has yet believed in God and the kingdom of God. No one has yet heard about the realm of the resurrection, not been homesick from that hour, waiting and looking forward joyfully to being released from bodily existence.
That life only really begins when it ends here on earth, and all that is here is only the prologue. So to my friend, everyone's friend, I say ting-a-ling, and Godspeed, my good friend.
The delegate from Prince William, Delegatory. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I'd like to speak to the motion made by the delegate from Chesapeake. The delegate has the floor. It was 2010.
I had a helicopter pilot and a gentleman who raised hogs, who had this very healthy mustache. And for 16 years, we served together.

General Laws, and we went back and forth over the last six years being chair of the House Appropriations Committee and on rules. Mr. Speaker has a saying that he often shares with me when we talk in private.

He says, we just got to get people to run the play. Delegate Knight and others who served in general laws and house appropriations, we would come together in our meetings and often congregate and talk about how we were going to run the play to make sure that we understood what we needed to do in order to advance legislation, in order to represent and to support the citizens of the Commonwealth of Virginia.

What many don't understand is that sometimes when you're Democrat or Republican, you have to come together and learn how to run the play for the betterment of the Commonwealth. And that is what we did. Mr. Speaker, oftentimes each day when I rise, I start my day listening to this song.
Great is thy faithfulness. And some of the lyrics, great is thy faithfulness. Morning by morning, new mercies I see. All I have needed, thy hand has provided.
Great is thy faithfulness, Lord, unto me. Great was God's faithfulness to Barry Knight. Morning by morning, God allowed him to see new mercies.
In all he needed, God hand provided for him. Great was God's faithfulness to delegate Barry Knight, my friend, Delores McQuinn's friend, our friend.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The delegate from Powhatan. Delegate Ware. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I join my colleagues in speaking of Barry Knight. The delegate has the floor. Barry's near neighbor in Virginia Beach, former Attorney General Jason Meares, captured the big picture, citing Teddy Roosevelt's son, who when his father passed said this, a great lion has passed.

I'm not sure I've ever known a man of greater accomplishment or less pretense. than Barry Knight. He was a delegate for 17 years. He served on the committees that have been alluded to, general laws, rules, ACNR, CCT, and on appropriations where he loomed larger and larger into the role of chairman. It is somehow fitting that he entered eternity on budget weekend.

He knew the waterfront of his beloved Virginia Beach, just as he came to know the complicated and interwoven waterfront of the Appropriations Territory. He came over time to an unparalleled command of its nuances.

And in that role, he befriended an array of folks, again, something that's been alluded to, and that array included people as different as Governor Yunkin and Senator Lucas. Amen. My first memory of Barry was him dropping his helicopter on a lawn at the 4-H Center at Smith Mountain Lake.

He and Paula and their three boys were attending that year's legislative trail ride. He could make an entrance. He would show up in that helicopter later at my little Powhatan courthouse backyard for an event.

And when he did, it became a modest Facebook sensation in my little corner of the world. But Barry could drive more than the helicopter. He could drive just about anything he sat in the seat of. He drove, as was mentioned, his Harley Davidson.

He drove a fuel oil tanker, a semi-long haul truck, a bulldozer, an excavator. I can't even name some of the other things he drove. And what's interesting is the only one that he actually took lessons for was the helicopter.

With the rest, he just climbed up on the seat or in the cab, fiddled with the instruments a little while, and off he went to drive them and operate them. But it was on his farm that the man in full appeared.

He knew and respected and loved the lineaments of the land, its waterways, and the buildings that came to serve him and his pigs. He was a hog farmer. And I suppose that's why, while he took life seriously, he never took himself too seriously.

I want you to picture this. You're at a reception, one of the receptions we go to around here. And a new acquaintance comes up to you and he asks, what do you do for a living outside the General Assembly? Hog farmer. Well, that's what it was for Barry.
It's also why he could see a project through, overcome roadblocks, and figure a way to solve often cross-grained problems, because that is the daily life of a farmer.

Comments yesterday alluded properly to his steadiness. He could be immovable, but he was only immovable after he'd heard out alternative and often conflicting views on things. He possessed a hard-earned capacity for judgment on property and policy and people.

In his chosen calling and in his life generally, Barry lived close to the fundamental things. You've heard from his early years how he loved to hunt and fish, and although his later accomplishments allowed him to hunt and fish in far-flung places, from Marathon in the Florida Keys to Casco Bay near Portland, Maine, from the forests of Virginia to the fields of South Dakota.

In keeping with those pastimes, he was an inveterate storyteller and joke teller. And sometime later, we can talk about some of those. Though he would travel, he was born and remained a son of Pungo, a rural community in Virginia Beach whose location and his district's location are in the very furthest, southeasternmost corner of this commonwealth of Virginia.

He did have to travel five miles to Creed to find Paula, and they were married together over 40 years. Together, they raised three very impressive sons. I hope you have the chance to meet them along the way.

And how many fathers do you know who've been asked to be the best man at their son's wedding? His faith, which he did not broadcast, but which he did live, was nurtured in the good Lord's great outdoors and in the Oak Grove Baptist Church.

He was a patriotic Virginian, and you've heard of his Jamestown ancestor. And I still recall, because I was there with him, his pleasure and his astonishment to be named to the Jamestown Yorktown Foundation Board. One of the greatest honors of my life has been to be Barry Knight's seatmate, which I have been for more than a decade, and to call him a friend.

The great Georgian writer Flannery O'Connor wrote, The writer operates at a peculiar crossroads where time and place and eternity somehow meet. Ms. Flannery's words also apply to the farmer who operates at the peculiar crossroads where time and place and eternity somehow meet.

Delegate Barry D. Knight entered eternity yesterday. And so, Mr. Speaker, I renew the motion of my colleagues that when the House adjourns today, it adjourns in the honor and memory of Delegate Barry D. Knight.

The delegates from Chesapeake, Delegate Leftwich, the delegate from Prince William, Delegate Torian, and the delegate from Powhatan, Delegate Webb, move that when the House adjourned today, it do so in the honor and memory of the Honorable Barry D. Knight.
All those in favor of the motion shall rise. The motion is agreed to.
Delegate from Virginia Beach. Delegate, ask you.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, I rise for the point of introduction. Delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, here today in the gallery, we have the senior adults living triumphantly of New Jerusalem Ministries. If they please rise.

Mr. Speaker, these dedicated members are led by our pastor, Dr. Veronica Coleman. New Jerusalem Ministries is the pillar of its community by bringing people together through fellowship, worship, and empowerment. Pastor Dr. Veronica Coleman and New Jerusalem Ministries grow through the study of God's word and serve in a valuable part of our community.
It is an honor to have them here today. My mother is up there as well, and I hope that the body will wish them a warm house welcome.

Welcome. Welcome to the Capitol today. The delegate from Colonial Heights, Delegate Cherry. Mr. Speaker, I rise for an announcement. Delegate has the floor. Mr. Speaker, even amongst the heaviness of today, it is a day of celebration for some, not only here in Virginia, but around the nation. Today, Mr. Speaker, is National Cherry Pie Day.

A few facts. Cherry trees made their way to Virginia in the 17th century. According to the USDA, there are 139 farms spanning 112 acres growing sweet, sweet cherries here in the Commonwealth. 67 farms on 24 acres growing sour cherries that we use in pies.

The majority of our cherry production lies in the southwest corner in Carroll and Patrick counties. I do need to acknowledge my colleague from Charlottesville. today for bringing this day to my attention and ensuring that we were so ready to celebrate. She even wore her cherry red shirt today, I will acknowledge.
Mr. Speaker, with my cherry tie, my cherry cup, my cherry socks, I enjoined my colleagues to please join me in the break room for some cherry pie. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Thank you, Delegate Cherry.

Delegate from Henrico, Delegate McQuinn. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, I rise for an announcement. Delegate has the floor. Mr. Speaker, I want to arise to remind my colleagues about the 18th annual Capitol Square Classic, House versus the Senate, which is February the 23rd on Monday.

The doors open at 5 p.m. and 7 p.m. is tip off at the Segal Center. But I also want to remind us that we're here and this is all about raising funds for the Massey Cancer Center, comprehensive cancer center.

And I'm hoping that this year, particularly as we have heard all that has been said about our colleague today, that we would give more now than we've ever given to help fight this good fight. It is a fight, and anyone who's diagnosed or who's struggling with cancer know the fight their families may be in, the communities.

So I'm asking you to please give the event is on Monday. We need you to please dig deep, as they say in the church, and dig deep so we could send a clear message in terms of this fight that we are contributors and we want to make a difference in the lives of those who are fighting every day, not just to live a quality of life, but just to live.

So thank you, Mr. Speaker. The delegate from Newport News, Delegate Price. Mr. Speaker, I rise for an introduction. Douglas, the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker and members. Today we have with us in the gallery special guests visiting from the Minority Political Leadership Institute, and I ask them to please stand.

This is a division of the L. Douglas Wilder School of Government and Public Affairs at the Grace E. Harris Leadership Institute at Virginia Commonwealth University. I had the pleasure of speaking to this group this year in November, and they asked thoughtful questions and are doing important work toward leadership development for those focused on issues important to minority communities including community economics, political climate, civic engagement and equity.

MPLI offers insights and concepts regarding personal leadership, policy and legislative processes to cultivate a deeper understanding of legacy, responsible stewardship, public service and integrity for future leaders from across the Commonwealth. Participants here today are not only learners, but also are leaders in their current fields and will continue to do work to shape Virginia's policies and progress for years to come. To the 2026 cohort of the Minority Political Leadership Institute, I hope it will be the pleasure of the body to give them a warm
house welcome. Welcome. Welcome to the Capitol today. Delegate from Shenandoah, Delegate Pence. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise for an announcement.

Delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It seems fitting today that I'd like to remind my colleagues that agriculture is the state's number one industry. And the number one organization advocating for agriculture is having their centennial celebration next Thursday, February 26th.

Mr. Speaker, Farm Bureau is celebrating their 100th anniversary. 100 years ago, the Speaker of the House was Democrat Thomas William Osland. And the 50th governor was Harry F. Byrd, Sr. And that year, the General Assembly passed 584 new laws, how things have changed.

Milk was 58 cents a gallon, bread was a dime a loaf, eggs were 56 cents a dozen, and bacon was 50 cents per pound. So, Mr. Speaker, you could have breakfast for a family of six for $1.75. Now that won't even buy you a cup of coffee. That's right. So in celebration of Farm Bureau Centennial, they're going to have a bus provided to take members of the General Assembly to their reception next Thursday at 5 p.m.

It'll be at the 9th Street Road there right between the parking garage and General Assembly Building. And they'll be featuring a reception featuring samplings from 14 districts all over the state. And I hope that you would enjoy participating with us, and we'll have you back here by 645 in time to put on your bowling shoes for the bipartisan bowling event that night.

So thank you, Mr. Speaker. The delegate from Virginia Beach, Delegate Converse Fowler. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise for an introduction. Delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, joining us in the gallery today is a group of Virginia Beach residents here for their Day of Action.

Mr. Speaker, in this group are members of the Virginia Beach Branch of the NAACP, Affordable Virginia, and Stand Up Now. I ask that they please rise if they are able. Mr. Speaker, these organizations and committed community members are focused on advancing equality, affordability, and a better life for all Virginians.

I hope that the members of the House will join me in giving them a warm House welcome. Welcome. Welcome to the Capitol today. Pursuant to House Rule 30, the journal shall reflect that the following members are away on pressing personal business on a granted leave from today's session.

Delegates Carroll, Clark, Maldonado, Rasul, and Ward. Clerk shall announce the next order of business. Mr. Speaker, the second portion of the morning hour reserve for announcements of member requests to move anything from an uncontested to a contested calendar. I'm not aware of any. Clerk will announce the next order of business.

Third portion of the morning hour reserve for member requests for an election to go by for the day. Similarly, I am not aware of any such requests. Clerk will announce the next order of business. And the fourth and final portion of the morning hour on this Friday is reserved for points of personal privilege. Kindly use your request to speak button to get into the queue. The delegate from Virginia Beach, Delegate Tater.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise for a point of personal privilege. The delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise to honor a giant of a man, Delegate Barry Knight. He was my friend, mentor, colleague, and brother in Christ. I've known Barry for almost 20 years, and there are simply no words adequate to express my love and admiration for such an extraordinary person in just two minutes.

But I want to share a few things that speak to why he meant so much to me. First, I've always believed that one of the truest measures of a man is how he treats and speaks about his wife. Barry adored Paula. He was a family-first man, and that began with his beloved wife.

I love that about him, and it is an incredible legacy he has passed on to his three boys. Second, you can tell a great deal about a person by how they handle adversity. Over the past couple of years in this body, Barry faced significant challenges. I spoke with him often during that time.

He was never angry or bitter. He would remind me almost routinely that he had his family, his true friends, and his faith, and that was enough. He was not defined by his position in the General Assembly, and he knew who he was, and he had his priorities straight.

And finally, he showed me how to live and how to die. He was taken far too soon, and his death still doesn't make sense to me. And yet, it is a stark reminder that we are here for just a brief time. The decisions we make, the way we treat people, it all matters.

I'm reminded of King David's words in Psalm 39. Lord, remind me how brief my time on earth will be. Remind me that my days are numbered, how fleeting my life is. You have made my life no longer than the width of my hand, and my entire lifetime is just a moment to you.

At best, each of us is just but a breath. Barry's life was fleeting, but I believe that when he left his earthly home, he did so with his integrity, his character, and his kindness. and his forgiving heart fully intact. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Delegate from Fauquier County, Delegate Weber.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, I rise for a point of personal privilege. Delegate has the floor. Mr. Speaker, today his desk in this chamber sits empty, and that emptiness carries weight.
He was the old guard, the grizzled lion, the kind of man whose respect was earned and not easily given. So was his loyalty.
Barry Knight was cut from a different cloth, a farmer first, A man shaped by hard seasons and long days. He had seen the world evolve, policy trends come and go, watched politics change.
But he never lost hold of where he came from. The hard days of his youth, the discipline of the work before dawn, the understanding that nothing worth building comes easy.

That life, lived hard and lived well, became a steady hand for this commonwealth. He produced food before he produced budgets. He understood stewardship long before he chaired appropriations. And when he became the senior delegate from Virginia Beach and chairman of appropriations, he did not view power as something to wield for show.

He understood it as responsibility. He respected the numbers because he respected the people behind those numbers. Barry was a student of the game, Mr. Speaker. He knew the inquiries of finance and the state budget not because it was glamorous, but because it mattered.

When he spoke, you listened. You really didn't have a choice. There was always something to learn from a man who had both dirt under his fingernails and command of the balance sheet. He was larger than life.

So was his love for his family. And he enjoyed being larger than life. The stories usually involved a helicopter ride, a hunting trip, Buddy Fowler, or fishing somewhere most of us had only read about. But the story that always makes me smile, I shared on social media.

I got a call from Barry one day asking what I knew about Deutz engines. He was looking at a tractor and wanted my opinion. I told him I thought they were solid engines, dependable, low maintenance. He said, good, I'm flying up there to take a look at a tractor.
